findings.title: Recovery codes sent to user storage as plaintext, bypassing hashing
findings.body: The user-storage path sends the raw generated codes as JSON through updateCredential. The local path stores hashed codes via createCredential. Federated storage therefore receives plaintext recovery codes, and validation compares plaintext too. This is a security regression for any storage provider that persists the value as given. The `credentialModel` already holds hashed data and could be used instead.

findings.title: Federated recovery credential never gets consumed or removed
findings.body: After a successful login, RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential may return a federated credential. Nothing marks the used code as consumed in user storage, so codes remain reusable. When allCodesUsed() is true, removeStoredCredentialById is called with a federated credential id and does not remove it from the user storage. One-time recovery codes then become reusable for federated users.

findings.title: Unchecked Optional.get() throws NoSuchElementException
findings.body: `credentialModelOpt.get()` is called without checking presence. If neither user storage nor local storage has the credential, this throws NoSuchElementException and the login form fails with an unhelpful error.

findings.title: Test storage rebuilds the recovery credential and loses its id
findings.body: getCredentials builds a new model through createFromValues, which hashes the raw codes and generates no id. The stored id (recoveryCodesModel.setId) is discarded. Also, isValid compares the input to the plaintext codes, while the model returned from getCredentials holds hashed codes. getCredentials can also NPE when myUser is null.
